summary.text: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, a cyan-coloured ice giant made mostly of water, ammonia and methane in a supercritical phase.
Its axis is tilted 82.23°, so over its 84-Earth-year orbit each pole gets about 42 years of sunlight, then 42 years of darkness.
It has the lowest minimum temperature of any planet, 49 K (-224 °C), and has been visited only once, by Voyager 2 in 1986.

items.prompt: You stand at a pole of Uranus. What does the Sun do over its 84-year orbit?

options.label: Shines nonstop for about 42 years, then vanishes for about 42
Rises and sets every 17 hours all year round
Shines for half of each year and sets for the rest
Never shines at all on the poles

items.explain: With a tilt of 82.23°, each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of continuous darkness.

items.prompt: Uranus can be seen with the naked eye, yet ancient observers never counted it as a planet. Why?

options.label: It hides behind Saturn's rings
It is visible only from the southern hemisphere
It is so bright that it looked like a comet
It is so dim and slow that it was taken for a star

items.explain: Because of its dimness and slow orbit it was never recognised as a planet, and earlier sightings were misidentified as stars.

items.prompt: Herschel called his new object a comet. What convinced others it was a planet?

options.label: Its nearly circular orbit
A long glowing tail pointing away from the Sun
A sudden brightening as it neared Earth
Its high speed across the background stars

items.explain: Lexell's computation showed a nearly circular orbit, which suggested a planet rather than a comet.

items.prompt: Compared with the other giant planets, how much heat comes from inside Uranus, and is the reason known?

options.label: A great deal, from a huge rocky core
Very little, because it is farthest of all from the Sun
Very little, and the cause remains unclear
The same as the others, and the cause is known

items.explain: It has very low internal heat compared to other giant planets, the cause of which remains unclear.

items.prompt: Uranus's rings reflect only a sliver of light. What may help darken them?

options.label: Black dust shed by its many inner moons
Charged particles in its lopsided magnetosphere
Soot thrown out by erupting volcanoes
The long shadow of the planet falling on them

items.explain: The highly asymmetric magnetosphere has many charged particles, which may be the cause of the darkening of the rings and moons.

items.prompt: Models of Uranus's interior put a thick hydrogen and helium envelope on the outside. What do they place below it?

options.label: A volatile mantle around a rocky core
A single solid ball of iron
An ocean of liquid metallic hydrogen
An empty cavity at the centre

items.explain: Inside its volatile mantle layer is a rocky core, and a thick hydrogen and helium atmosphere surrounds it.
